Meeting Schedule

The regular meetings of the City Council are held on the second and fourth Tuesday of each month,

  1
 closed session business will usually commence at 5:30 p.m., when scheduled, and general business
session will commence at 6:30 p.m.

Brown Act

Agendas are drafted to accurately state what the legislative body is being asked to consider. The
legislative body can take action on "all items" listed on the agenda and be in compliance with the open
meeting laws. Under the Brown Act, no action may be taken on a matter unless it is listed on the
agenda, or unless certain emergency or special circumstances exist. The governing body may direct
staff to investigate and/or schedule certain matters for consideration at a future meeting.

City's Vision Statement

We envision a thriving, safe and inclusive community where everyone has the opportunity to access
exceptional services, education and support to be resilient and live full, vibrant lives.

Public Communications

Public Comments on agenda items are limited to three (3) minutes. All comments are to be addressed
directly to the Agency Members not to the members of the public.

summarized by the City Clerk, not read in its entirety. A copy of the email will be provided to the City
Council and will also be available at the City Clerk's Office for public review. A copy of each email will be

 GENERAL NOTICE TO THE PUBLIC

The City Council adopted new rules relating to the conduct of the public meetings, proceedings, and
business in the City of South Gate on July 12, 2022, (Resolution 2022-38-CC) and go into effect on
August 1, 2022. Resolution #2022-38-CC is available at the City Clerk’s Office.

MEETING SCHEDULE

Regular meetings of the City Council are held on the second and fourth Tuesday of each month, closed
session meetings will commence at 5:30 p.m. unless posted otherwise on its agenda. The regular City
Council meetings will commence at 6:30 p.m. Agendas are available at the following locations: City Clerk
Office, Public Notice Boards at City Hall, and on the City’s web page at https://www.cityofsouthgate.org

The Public can sign up to receive automatic notices of postings of agendas for the City Council or any
other Commission or Board of the City of South Gate. Visit the City webpage and click on the Agenda &
Minutes icon. That will take you the page where an individual can enter their email in the “Email
Updates” box to register.

PUBLIC COMMENT/PARTICIPATION

Any person may request to address a legislative body during a public meeting. The Presiding Officer will
call upon those present in the Council Chambers.

Speakers are limited to three (3) minutes on any item listed on the agenda, including public hearings.
Under Comments from the Audience portion, speakers are also limited to a single three (3) minutes time
limit. Comments from the Audience is initially limited to 45 minutes at each meeting. Any speaker still
wishing to speak, that did not speak, will have an addition Comments from the Audience opportunity after
the last business item is finished. The Presiding Officer may extend the time limit as long as there is no
objection from the City Council as a body.

To ensure that the public is able to participate, the City provides the opportunity to submit their
comments in person, email, mail. Methods of participation may be subject to change during other such
times when a State of Emergency, Health Order or State Executive Order limits in-person participation.

CURFEW

In absence of a motion duly adopted by majority vote of the City Council, the Presiding Officer may
adjourn the City Council meetings at 10:30 p.m. The Presiding Officer may ask the City Council if any
agenda items listed should be continued or dealt with during the meeting. For those items to be
continued, the City Council can direct the item be placed on the next City Council agenda or the current
meeting may be adjourned to a time certain at which time the meeting shall be reconvened as an
Adjourned Regular Meeting of the City Council and action upon the published agenda continued.

STAFF REPORTS

As a general rule, staff reports. or other written documentation are prepared/organized with respect to
each item of business listed on the agenda. Meeting agendas and staff reports are available at least 72-
hours prior to the scheduled regular City Council meeting and a minimum of 24-hours prior to a Special
City Council meeting. There are times when the City Council receives written material. revised material
after the posting of agendas, these materials are become a public record and will be available for public
view within 72-hours after the meeting in which they were received. Those materials and any other public
document can be inspected in the City Clerk's Office located at 8650 California Avenue, South Gate.

SERVICES TO FACILITATE ACCESS TO PUBLIC MEETINGS

  8
 In compliance with the American with Disabilities Act, if you need special assistance to participate in the

Council Meeting will enable the City to make reasonable arrangements to assure accessibility. For
further information, please contact the Office of the City Clerk at (323) 563-9510 or via email at
yglaze@sogate.org.

  SUBJECT:  CITY  OF SOUTH  GATE  2025  PUBLIC  HEALTH  GOALS  REPORT  ON
  DRINKING  WATER  QUALITY

  PURPOSE:  To approve  the receiving  and filing  of the City  of South  Gate 2025 Public  Health
  Goals Report  ("PHG  Report")  as required  by the California  Health  and Safety  Code.

  RECOMMENDED  ACTIONS:  Following  the  conclusion  of the public  hearing,  the  City
  Council  will  consider  receiving  and filing  the  City  of South  Gate  2025  Public  Health  Goals
  ("PHG")  Report,  as required  by the California  Health  and Safety  Code.

  FISCAL  IMPACT:  There  is no fiscal  impact  to the General  Fund.  The cost to prepare  the
  2025 PHG Report  was $3,800,  which  was funded  through  the Water  Fund.

  NOTICING  PROCEDURES:  A notice  of the public  hearing  was published  in the South  Gate
  Press  on July  24, 2025, and the PHG Report  was posted  on the City  of South  Gate's  ("City")
  website  in accordance  with  public  noticing  requirements.

  ANALYSIS:  The  California  Health  and  Safety  Code,  Section  116470,  requires  public  water
  systems  with  more  than 10,000  service  connections  to prepare  a PHG  Report  every  three years.
  This report  explains  the levels  of certain  constituents  in the City's  drinking  water that have PHGs
  or Maximum  Contaminant  Level  Goals  ("MCLGs")  but do not have  enforceable  water  quality
  standards.

  The City's  water  system  serves over 14,300  connections  and meets  all state and federal  drinking
  water  quality  standards.  While  a few compounds  were detected  above the PHG  or MCLG  levels,
  they  remained  well  below  the enforceable  regulatory  limits  established  to ensure  safe drinking
  water.  That said, water  served to customers  meets  State and Federal  Drinking  Water  Standards.

  The  most  notable  compounds  are Per-  and Polyfluoroalkyl  Substances  ("PFAS").  To  address
  this, the City  is designing  a water  treatment  plant  specifically  to remove  PFAS  compounds.  This
  proactive  approach  goes  beyond  current  regulatory  requirements  and demonstrates  the  City's
  commitment  to maintaining  water  quality  that exceeds  minimum  safety  standards.

  For  the  other  compounds  included  in the  PHG  Report,  meeting  PHG  levels  would  require
  extensive  new  treatment  facilities  and  higher  operational  costs,  which  would  significantly

  1

  10
 increase  costs  for  ratepayers.  Because  the  City's  water  already  meets  all  state  and  federal
drinking  water  quality  standards,  and PHGs  are non-enforceable  health-based  guidelines,  no
additional  treatment  is recornrnended  at this time.

Any  and all :tundings  in the PHG  Report  demonstrates  how  water  served  to customers  meets
State and Federal  Drinking  Water  Standards.  It is noted  that all water  quality  data summarized
in the  PHG  Report  is also  available  in  the  2024  Annual  Water  Quality  Report  (Consumer
Confidence  Report),  which  is posted  on the City's  website  for public  access.

BACKGROUND:  The City's  municipal  water  system  provides  drinking  water  that meets  all
state and federal  drinking  water  quality  standards.  To ensure  continued  compliance  with  these
regulations  and to protect  public  health,  the City  collects  and analyzes  over 2,000  water  samples
every  year. These  samples  are tested  for a wide  range of water  quality  indicators  to confirm  that
the City's  water  is safe to drink  and consistently  meets regulatory  standards.

Every  three years,  the City  is required  to prepare  a PHG Report,  which  summarizes  the results  of
water  quality  testing  for  certain  compounds  in drinking  water.  The  2025  PHG  Report  reflects
data collected  in 2022,  2023,  and 2024  for ten compounds  that have been assigned  either  PHGs
by the State of California  or MCLGs  by the U.S. Environmental  Protection  Agency.

It is important  to note  that  PHGs  and  MCLGs  are not  enforceable  water  quality  standards.
Instead,  they  represent  health-based  goals,  which  are levels  at which  a contaminant  is not
expected  to cause  adverse  health  effects  over  a lifetime  of exposure.  The  enforceable  water
quality  standards  are called  Maximum  Contaminant  Levels  ("MCLs"),  which  are set to ensure
water  remains  safe to drink.  The City's  water  supply  meets all MCLs,  meaning  that South  Gate's
drinking  water  is safe and in full  compliance  with  state and federal  requirements.

The  City's  public  water  system  is a vital  utility  that  supports  the  community  every  day.  It
includes:

  *  14,300serviceconnectionsservingover90%oftheCity'sresidentsandbusinesses

  135 miles  of water pipelines  delivering  safe drinking  water  throughout  the City

  *  Six active  water  wells  and six water  reservoirs  with  a combined  storage  capacity  of more
  than 14 million  gallons

  *  Approximately  3,500  water  valves,  which  allow  staff  to operate,  maintain,  and isolate
  portions  of the system  as needed

This  extensive  water  system  allows  the  City  to reliably  provide  clean  drinking  water  to its
residents  while  meeting  all  regulatory  requirements.  The  PHG  Report  is part  of  the  City's
ongoing  commitment  to transparency  and public  health,  providing  residents  and decision-makers
with  clear information  about water  quality  and the City's  efforts  to maintain  it.

1.0  Introduction

Under  the Calderon-Sher  Safe  Drinking  Water  Act of 1996  public  water  systems  in California

serving  greater  than 10,000  service  connections  must prepare  a report  containing  information

on 1) detection  of any contaminant  in drinking  water  at a level exceeding  a Public  Health  Goal

(PHG),  2) estimate  of costs  to remove  detected  contaminants  to below  the PHG  using  Best

Available  Technology  (BAT),  and 3) health  risks for each contaminant  exceeding  a PHG.  This

report must be made available  to the public every three years.  The initial PHGs Report was due

on July 1, 1998, and subsequent  reports  are due every three years thereaffer.

The 2025  PHGs  Report  has been  prepared  to address  the requirements  set forth  in Section

116470  of the California  Health  and Safety  Code.  It is based  on water quality  analyses  during

calendar  years  2022,  2023,  and 2024 or, if certain  analyses  were  not performed  during  those

years,  the most  recent  data  is used.  The 2025  PHGs  Report  has been  designed  to be as

imormative  as  possible,  without  unnecessary  duplication  of  information  contained  in the

Consumer  Confidence  Report  (also  known  as Water  Quality  Report),  which  was  mailed  to

customers  by July 1 of each year.

There  are  no regulations  explaining  requirements  for the  preparation  of PHGs  reports.  A

workgroup  of the Association  of California  Water  Agencies  (ACWA)  Water  Quality  Committee

has prepared  suggested  guidelines  for water  utilities  to use in preparing  PHGs  reports.  The

ACWA  guidelines  were  used in the preparation  of this 2025  PHGs  Report.  These  guidelines

include  tables  of cost estimates  for BAT.  The State  of California  (State)  provides  ACWA  with

numerical  health  risks and category  of health  risk information  for contaminants  with PHGs.  This

health risk information  is appended  to the ACWA  guidelines.

2.O  California  Drinking  Water  Regulatoiy  Process

California  Health  and Safety  Code  Section  116365  requires  the State  to develop  a PHG for

every  contaminant  with a primary  drinking  water  standard  or for any contaminant  the State  is

City of South Gate  1  2025 PHGs Report

  13
 proposing  to  regulate  with  a primary  drinking  water  standard.  A  PHG  is the  level  of  a

contaminant  in drinking  water  that  poses  no significant  health  risk if consumed  for a lifetime.

The  process  of establishing  a PHG  is a risk  assessment  based  strictly  on  human  health

considerations.  PHGs  are recommended  targets  and  are not required  to be met by any public

water  system.

The  State  office  designated  to  develop  PHGs  is the  California  Environmental  Protection

Agency's  Office  of  Environmental  Health  Hazard  Assessment  (OEHHA).  The  PHG  is then

forwarded  to the State  Water  Resources  Control  Board,  Division  of Drinking  Water  (DD\/V)  for

use in revising  or developing  a Maximum  Contaminant  Level  (MCL)  in drinking  water.  The  MCL

is the highest  level  of a contaminant  that  is allowed  in drinking  water.  State  MCLs  cannot  be

less  stringent  than  federal  MCLs  and  must  be as  close  as  is technically  and  economically

feasible  to the  PHGs.  DDW  is required  to take  treatment  technologies  and cost  of compliance

into account  when  setting  an MCL.  Each  MCL is reviewed  at least once  every  five years.

Two  radiological  contaminants  (gross  alpha  particle  activity  and  gross  beta  particle  activity)

have  MCLs  but do  not yet  have  designated  PHGs.  For these  contaminants,  the  Maximum

Contaminant  Level  Goal  (MCLG),  the federal  u.s.  Environmental  Protection  Agency  (USEPA)

equivalent  of PHGs,  is used  in the 2025  PHGs  Report.

3.0  Identification  of Contaminants

Section  116470(b)(1)  of the  Health  and  Safety  Code  requires  public  water  systems  serving

more  than  10,000  service  connections  to identify  each  contaminant  detected  in drinking  water

that  exceeded  the  applicable  PHG.  Section  116470(f)  requires  the  MCLG  to  be  used  for

comparison  if there  is no applicable  PHG.

The City of South  Gate  (City)  water  system  has approximately  14,442  service  connections.  The

following  constituents  were  detected  at one  or more  locations  within  the drinking  water  system

at levels  that exceeded  the applicable  PHGs  or MCLGs:

  *  Arsenic  - naturally-occurring  in local  groundwater.

7.O  Costs  of Using  Best Available  Technologies  and Intended  Actions

Section  11 6470(b)(5)  of the Health  and Safety  Code requires  an estimate  of the aggregate  cost

and  cost  per  customer  of utilizing  the  BATs  identified  to  reduce  the  concentration  of a

contaminant  to a level  at or below  the  PHG  or MCLG.  In addition,  Section  116470(b)(6)

requires  a brief  description  of any  actions  the water  purveyor  intends  to take to reduce  the

concentration  of the contaminant  and the basis for that decision.

The  City  operates  one  Spray  Aeration  Treatment  System  installed  in the  South  Gate  Park

Reservoir  for the treatment  of PCE  and TCE detected  in the local groundwater  at four of the

City's water supply  wells.

Arsenic  - The  BATs  for removal  of arsenic  in water  for large  water  systems  are: activated

alumina,  coagulation/Filtration,  electrodialysis,  ion exchange,  lime soffening,  oxidation/Filtration,

and reverse  osmosis.  Arsenic  was detected  above the PHG in the local groundwater.  The City

is in compliance  with the MCL for arsenic.  The estimated  cost to reduce  arsenic  levels in local

groundwater to below the PHG of O.004 microgram per liter (4g/1) using ion exchange was
calculated.  Because  the DDW  detection  limit for purposes  of reporting  (DLR)  for arsenic  is 2

pg/1, treating  arsenic  to below the PHG level means  treating  arsenic  to below the DLR of 2 pg/1.

There  are numerous  factors  that may influence  the actual  cost of reducing  arsenic  levels to the

  Homes  constructed  before 1980;

  Water  supplied  to the home is naturally  soff or corrosive;  or

  Stagnant  water  in the household  plumbing  for several  hours or longer.

  substance, or the source must be removed from service.

  In order to ensure that tap water is safe to drink, the U. S. Environmental Protection Agency (USEPA)and the State Water Resources Control
  Board (State Water Board) prescribe regulations that limit the amount of certain contaminants in water provided by public water systems.

ANALYSIS:  Proposed  Third  Amendment  to Contract  No.  2940  updates  the Memorandum  of
Understanding  ("MOU")  with  the  Gateway  Water  Management  Authority  ("GWMA")  to
continue  supporting  the  preparation  of  the Lower  Los  Angeles  River  ("LLAR")  Watershed
Management  Program  ("WMP")  and  Coordinated  Integrated  Monitoring  Program  ("CIMP").
This  amendment  serves  as the City's  vehicle  to cost-share  with  participating  LLAR  watershed
agencies  for  the technical  work  required  to comply  with  regional  stormwater  regulations.  By
collaborating  with  neighboring  cities  through  this  MOU,  the  City  can  meet  the  complex
monitoring  and reporting  requirements  of the 2021  Municipal  Separate  Storm  Sewer  System
(MS4)  Permit  at  a  significantly  reduced  cost  compared  to  completing  these  studies
independently.  Key updates  in the proposed  amendment  include:

  *  Extending  the MOU  term  for five  years,  from  October  1, 2025,  through  September  30,
  2030,  or until  the expiration  of the next MS4  permit,  whichever  occurs  first.

  @  Clarifying  that  funds  collected  under  the  MOU  may  be  used  for  regional  Best
  Management  Practice  ("BMP")  projects  agreed  upon  by  the  LLAR  Watershed
  Permittees.

  *  Incorporating  GWMA's  administrative  cost recovery  program  to ensure  administrative
  expenses  are properly  funded.

  *  Updating  the cost-share  formula  for the WMP,  CIMP,  and any other  approved  regional
  expenditures,  all subject  to annual  budget  approval.

  *  GWMA  will  continue  serving  as the fiduciary  agency,  managing  consultant  contracts  for
  monitoring  and  scientific  studies,  awarding  special  studies,  and  administering
  construction  contracts  for regional  projects.

  *  LA  County  Flood  Control  District's  cost  share  remains  5%,  as it participates  in  all
  watersheds  within  the County.

  Any  permittee  may  withdraw  with  30  days'  notice  but  remains  responsible  for  its
  proportional  share  of  any  costs  GWMA  has  incurred  or  committed  to  through  the
  effective  date of withdrawal.

By  participating  in  this  regional  cost-sharing  agreement,  the  City  meets  its  MS4  Permit
requirements  in  the  most  efficient  and  cost-effective  manner,  avoiding  significantly  higher
expense  of performing  all required  stormwater  monitoring  and studies  independently.

The  total  budget  to fund  the WMP  and CIMP  activities  estimated  over  the next  five  years  is
$4,026,415.  The City's  share will  be $631,430,  which  requires  an annual  payment  of $126,286.

 BACKGROUND:  The City  of South  Gate's  storm  drain  system  is regulated  under  the National
Pollutant  Discharge  Elimination  System  ("NPDES")  Municipal  Separate  Storm  Sewer  System
(MS4)  Permit,  issued by the State Water  Resources  Control  Board  in 2012 (Order  No. R4-2012-
0175).  This  permit  requires  cities  in Los  Angeles  County  to manage  all stormwater  and non-
stormwater  discharges  in a way  that protects  water  quality.  Under  the MS4  Permit,  cities  must
develop  and implement  two key programs:

  1.  Watershed  Management  Program  ("WMP")  - A plan to reduce  pollutants  in stormwater
  throughout  the watershed.

  2.  Coordinated  Integrated  Monitoring  Program  ("CIMP")  - A monitoring  plan  to measure
  water  quality  improvements  and ensure compliance  with  the permit.

The greatest  challenge  for cities  is the cost of implementing  these programs.  Complying  with  the
MS4  Permit  independently  is cost-prohibitive,  which  is why  South  Gate and neighboring  cities
chose to work  together  under  a Memorandum  of Understanding  ("MOU")  administered  by the
GWMA.  This  regional  cost-sharing  approach  allows  cities  to  meet  permit  requirements
efficiently  and at a much  lower  cost than pursuing  compliance  alone.

The  GWMA  MOU  (Contract  No.  2940)  was first  approved  by the City  Council  on September
10, 2013,  creating  a partnership  of LLAR  Watershed  Permittees,  which  includes  the cities  of
Downey,  Lakewood,  Long  Beach,  Lynwood,  Paramount,  Pico  Rivera,  Signal  Hill,  South  Gate,
and the Los Angeles  County  Flood  Control  District.

Subsequent  amendments  to the MOU  refined  the scope and cost-sharing  approach:

  *  First  Amendment  (August  11, 2015)  - Added  WMP  and CIMP  implementation  to the
  MOU  and established  a cost-sharing  formula  of 80% by land area and 20%  equally  split
  among  the LLAR  Permittees.

  *  Second  Amendment  (August  25, 2020)  - Extended  the MOU  to September  30, 2025,  and
  revised  the cost-share  to 90% by land area and 10% equally  split.

The WMP  and CIMP  provide  a roadmap  to reduce  pollutants  in the Lower  Los Angeles  River
and  its  tributaries.  A  key  component  of  these  plans  is the  Reasonable  Assurance  Analysis
("RAA"),  which  evaluates  stormwater  runoff  and  determines  the  optimal  combination  of
treatment  projects  and  timelines  to  meet  MS4  Permit  goals.  The  RAA  also  distributes  the
responsibility  for constructing  treatment  facilities  among  all participating  agencies.

Based  on the RAA,  South  Gate is required  to treat 168 acre-feet  of stormwater  at an estimated
cost of $61 million  by 2028.  By participating  in the GWMA  MOU,  the City  is able to share these
costs with  neighboring  cities,  ensuring  regulatory  compliance  at an affordable  cost.

 ANALYSIS:  The  Urban  Orchard  Project  reached  substantial  completion  and  opened  to the
public  in  July  2025.  This  $30 million  project  introduced  numerous  recreational  amenities,
including  an Education  Building  and a combined  Garage/Restroom  Building.  Both  facilities  were
designed  to include  alarm  systems  to protect  City  of South  Gate ("City")  assets from  vandalism
and unauthorized  access.

Security  for  City  facilities  is a longstanding  priority.  The  City  currently  operates  54 facilities,
many  of which  are equipped  with  a combination  of burglar  alarms,  access controls,  and closed-
circuit  television  ("CCTV")  systems.  These  systems  are installed  and monitored  by SSD, which
has provided  reliable  security  services  for critical  facilities  such as City  Hall,  the Civic  Center,
and the Public  Works  Corporate  Yard.

To ensure  continuity  in security  operations  and simplify  monitoring,  staff  recommends  utilizing
SSD to install  and monitor  alarm  systems  for the new Urban  Orchard  facilities.  Amendment  No.
2 to the Agreement  provides  for such. It includes  two  cost components:  a one-time  installation
cost is $12,171, with  an ongoing  annual  monitoring  fee of $4,356.

BACKGROUND:  The City  operates  54 facilities  where  security  is a top priority.  Over the years,
the City  has implemented  and expanded  security  measures  to meet evolving  needs. Key  facilities
such as City  Hall,  the Civic  Center,  and the Public  Works  Corporate  Yard  are equipped  with
burglar  alarms,  access controls,  and CCTV  systems.

Since  2004,  SSD has provided  the City  with  security  services,  including  burglar  alarms,  CCTV
systems,  and ongoing  monitoring.  SSD currently  services  24 buildings  under  41 active  accounts,
with  all contracts  structured  to expire  at the end of the fiscal  year to allow  for flexibility  should
the City  transition  to a new provider.  In accordance  with  South  Gate Municipal  Code  Sections
1.54.510.A  and 1.54.510.H,  the City  is authorized  to enter  into  contracts  directly  with  SSD to
maintain  standardized  security  operations  without  the need for public  bidding.

SSD has provided  services  to the City  since 2004.  SSD provides  burglar  alarm  services,  closed-
circuit  television  security  systems,  other  security  systems  and services  to the City  at numerous
City-owned  buildings,  parks  and other facilities.  The total  in annual  monitoring  fees paid to SSD
is $4356,  for the existing  systems.

There  are two  cost components  to SSD contracts:  (1) equipment  and installation  costs  and (2)
monitoring  costs.  Equipment  and installation  costs are one-time  costs and monitoring  costs are
annual  costs. The proposed  fee for equipment  and installation  costs is $12,171 and the proposed
aru'iual monitoring  cost is $4,356.

PURPOSE:  To amend  current  three-year  agreement  No.  2022-65-CC  with  Melad  and Associates,
Inc. and No. 2022-66-CC  with  True North  Compliance  Services  to extend  two additional  years for plan

RECOMMENDED  ACTIONS:
  a.  Approve  Amendment  No.  I to Agreements  with  Melad  and Associates,  Inc.  and True  North
  Compliance  Services  to provide  plan  check  and building  inspection  services  in the amount  not
  to exceed  $1,500,000,  over  a two-year  extension  term,  funds  allocation  starting  July  1, 2025
  until  September  30, 2027;  and
  b.  Authorize  the Mayor  to execute  the Agreement  in a form  acceptable  to the City  Attorney;

included  in the FY 2025-2026  budget  and will  be offset  by revenues  from  plan check  fees, with  Melad
and Associates,  Inc;  and True North  Compliance  Services  retaining  65%  of plan  check  fees collected
by the City.

ALIGNMENT  WITH  COUNCIL  GOALS:  The  proposed  Amendment  supports  the City  Council
goals  of "encouraging  economic  development"  and "development  and protecting  strong  sustainable
neighborhoods  " This  is accomplished  by providing  high  quality  plan  check  services  that ensure  new
construction  is designed  to meet  safety  standards  with  the City's  Building  Code.  In addition,  plan
check  services  will  continue  to be provided  in a short  period  of time  to benefit  residents,  investors,
developers  and contractors.  Another  City  Council  goal is to enhance,  accelerate  and update  services  to
the latest  technology  available  such  as electronic  plan  check  to expedite  the plan  check  process  for
investors,  developers,  contractors,  homeowners  and the general  public,  and Melad  and Associates  Inc.,
and True North  Compliance  Services  will  help achieve  this City  Council  goal.

ANALYSIS:  To ensure the City  continues  to receive  high  quality  building  plan check  services  at the
most  competitive  cost,  a contract  was  awarded  to  Melad  and  Associates,  Inc;  and  True  North
Compliance  Services  in October  1, 2022  for  three  years  with  an option  to extend  the contract  two

  RECOMMENDED  ACTIONS:  The City  Council  will  consider:
  a.  Authorizing  purchasing  six (6) 2025  Ford  F-150  Lightning  trucks  from  National  Auto
  Fleet  Group,  utilizing  the Sourcewell  Co-Op  Purchasing  Program  in an amount  not-to-
  exceed  $385,032,  or $64,172  pertruck,,
  b.  Appropriating  $128,344  in Water  Funds  to fully  fund the purchase  of two  (2) Ford F-150
  Lightning's  for the Public  Works,  Water  Division;  and
  c.  Authorizing  the  City  Manager  to  execute  the  documents  necessary  to  complete  the
  purchase  transactions  to acquire  the trucks  in forms  acceptable  to the City  Attorney.

  FISCAL  IMPACT:  There  is no impact  to the General  Fund.  The purchase  cost of four  (4) 2025
  Lightning  Trucks  is $256,688  to be funded  with  Capital  Asset  and  Equipment  Replacement
  ("CAER")  Funds  budgeted  in the Fiscal  Year  2025/26  0perating  Budget.  An  appropriation  of
  $128,344  in Water  Funds  (Account  411-731-71-9003)  is recommended  to :tully fund and purchase
  two (2) additional  2025 Lightning  Trucks  for the Water  Division.

  ANALYSIS:  The Public  Works  Department  relies  on its Street  and Sewer  Division  and Water
  Division  to maintain  critical  infrastructure  and respond  to resident  needs every  day.  The Street
  and  Sewer  Division  maintains  streets,  including  asphalt  and  concrete  repairs,  street  sign

  replacement,  bulky  item  cleanups,  sewer  system  upkeep,  and tree  maintenance.  The  Water
  Division  operates  and maintains  the City's  water  system,  performing  tasks such as replacing  water
  valves  and responding  to emergencies  like broken  water  mains  or damaged  fire hydrants.  These
  operations  depend  on reliable  vehicles  and equipment  to ensure crews  can work  safely,  efficiently,
  and without  interruption.

  The vehicles  currently  serving  these divisions  have exceeded  their  useful  life,  resulting  in more
  frequent  breakdowns,  higher  maintenance  costs,  and increased  fuel  consumption  and emissions.

  I

  75
 Replacing  these aging vehicles  will  improve  operational  efficiency,  reduce maintenance  costs, and
support  the Department's  ability  to deliver  the high level  of service  residents  expect  every  day.

Staff  is proposing  to replace  six (6) aging  vehicles  with  upgraded  2025 Lightning  Truck  electric
vehicle  models.  Transitioning  to electric  vehicles  will  significantly  reduce  fuel  consumption,
lower  emissions,  and decrease  maintenance  costs compared  to the older  gasoline-powered  units
they will  replace.  This approach  not only  improves  operational  efficiency  but also aligns  with  the
California  Air  Resources  Board  ("CARB")  requirements  for alternative-fuel  vehicle  purchases,
supporting  the City's  commitment  to sustainability

Staff  recornrnends  purchasing  the  2025  Lightning  Trucks  through  the  cooperative  contract
purchasing  program  offered  by  Sourcewell  (formerly  known  as the  National  Joint  Powers
Alliance),  under  contract  #091521-NAF.  This program  leverages  the national  purchasing  power
of over 50,000  member  agencies,  streamlining  the procurement  process  and reducing  the time and
effort  required  for the City.  Sourcewell  establishes  and provides  competitively  solicited  contracts
in accordance  with  the Uniform  Municipal  Contracting  Law,  ensuring  compliance  with  legal and
competitive  standards.  This  method  of purchasing  aligns  with  the City  of South  Gate's  ("City")
Municipal  Code  requirements  outlined  in Section  1.54.510D,  which  allows  the City  to utilize
contracts  established  by other government  agencies,  avoiding  the need to repeat  the competitive
bidding  process.

BACKGROUND:  The  Public  Works  Department  operates  a fleet  of  90 vehicles  that  are
essential  for  maintaining  and operating  the City's  infrastructure.  The reliability  of this  fleet  is
critical  to ensuring  timely  response  to resident  needs, efficient  service  delivery,  and proper  upkeep
of City  streets,  sewers,  and the municipal  water  system.

To guide the management  of this fleet, the Department  prepared  a Fleet Master  Plan ("Plan")  with
the  goals  of  reducing  operating  and  maintenance  costs,  ensuring  safety  and  reliability,  and
optimizing  vehicle  productivity.  The  Plan  establishes  recornrnended  replacement  cycles  that
minimize  the total  cost of ownership  by replacing  vehicles  before  maintenance  costs, downtime,
and fuel consumption  rise significantly.

The vehicles  proposed  for replacement  in this report  have exceeded  their  recornrnended  service
life,  with  the Plan identi'fying  their  replacement  between  2019  and 2024.  Continuing  to operate
these  aging  vehicles  leads  to  higher  maintenance  costs,  increased  emissions,  and  reduced
reliability.  Replacing  them with  modern  units,  equipped  with  improved  safety  features  and fuel-
efficient  technology,  will  enhance  operational  efficiency  and reduce  long-term  costs.

Upon  Council  approval,  delivery  of the new vehicles  is expected  in approximately  16 weeks.  Once
delivered,  the units will  be outfitted  with  safety  lighting,  toolboxes,  and other required  equipment
before  being  placed  into service.

  FISCAL  IMPACT:  There is no impact  to the General  Fund.  The purchase  of one (1) John Deere
  320 P-Tier  Backhoe  Loader  is in the amount  of $182,906.  It is budgeted  in the Fiscal  Year 2025/26
  Operating  Budget  in the amount  of $180,040,  with  Water  funds  (Account  411-731-71-9003),  thus
  a $2,866  Water  Fund appropriation  is needed  to fully  fund its purchase.

  ANALYSIS:  The  Water  Division  is responsible  for  operating  and  maintairung  the  City's
  municipal  water  system,  which  provides  service  to both residential  and commercial  customers.  A
  critical  component  of this system  is the network  of water  mains  and valves  that distribute  water
  throughout  the community.  Maintenance  of these lines  often  requires  excavation  with  a backhoe
  loader  to safely  access underground  infrastructure.  There is a need to replace  the Water  Division's
  backhoe,  which  is Unit No. 352.

  Unit  No.  352, which  is 11 years old and currently  assigned  to the Water  Division,  is in reliable
  mechanical  condition  and has been well-maintained.  However,  it no longer  meets the operational
  demands  of the Water  Division,  which  includes  complex  and heavy-duty  work  associated  with
  water  system  construction,  repairs,  and emergency  response.  Despite  this, Unit  No. 352 remains
  serviceable  and is well-suited  for essential  tasks in the Streets  Division,  such as roadway  repairs,
  material  handling,  and general  maintenance.  For these reasons,  staff proposes  purchasing  a new

BACKGROUND:  The  Public  Works  Department  operates  a fleet  of 90 vehicles  that  are
essential  for maintaining  and operating  the City's  infrastructure,  including  streets,  sewers,  the
water  system,  and emergency  response  needs.  The reliability  of this  fleet  is critical  to ensuring
that crews can respond  promptly  to resident  service  requests,  perform  maintenance  efficiently,  and
address unplanned  emergencies  such as water  main breaks,  fallen  trees, or storm-related  debris.

To manage  the fleet and plan for vehicle  replacements,  the Department  developed  a Fleet Master
Plan ("Plan").  The Plan is designed  to reduce  overall  operating  and maintenance  costs, ensure the
safety  and reliability  of the  fleet,  and increase  operational  efficiency  by providing  the right
equipment  for each task. It also establishes  recommended  vehicle  replacement  cycles  that achieve
the lowest  total  cost of ownership.  Replacing  vehicles  at the appropriate  point  in their  lifecycle
avoids  the escalating  costs of operating  older units,  which  are prone to frequent  repairs,  increased
downtime,  higher  fuel  consumption,  and  greater  emissions.  Modern  vehicles  also  provide
enhanced  safety  features,  such as backup  cameras  and proximity  sensors, which  improve  operator
visibility  and  reduce  the risk  of  accidents.  Staff  follows  the Plan  as a guide  when  making
recommendations  to replace  vehicles.

That  said, the Streets  Division  currently  utilizes  a backhoe,  which  is Unit  No.  351, for  streets
maintenance  and repairs.  Unit  No.  351 is over 24 years old, has exceeded  its recommended  life
cycle,  and has become  increasingly  unreliable,  requiring  frequent  repairs.  In addition,  it is diesel-
powered  and does not meet current  emission  standards,  meaning  it must be removed  from  service
by 2032 under  California  Air Resources  Board  ("CARB")  regulations.  Given  its age, maintenance
costs, and air quality  impacts,  Unit  No.  351 was scheduled  for replacement  in 2019  according  to
the Fleet Master  Plan. Its continued  operation  is now well  beyond  its recommended  life cycle and
has become  increasingly  costly  and unreliable  to maintain.  Replacing  this unit  at this time  will
bring  the  fleet  into  closer  alignment  with  the  Plan,  reduce  long-term  costs,  and  ensure  the
Department  can continue  providing  efficient  and uninterrupted  service  to the community.  For this
reason,  Unit  No. 351 will  be retired  from  service  and sent to auction,  and replaced  with  Unit  No.
352.

  PURPOSE:  To approve purchasing one (l) 2024 Rizon Electric truck with 14" Stake Bed for
  the Department of Public Works Street and Sewer Division.

  RECOMMENDED  ACTIONS:  The  City  Council  will  consider:

  a.  Authorizingthepurchaseofone(l)RizonElectrictnickwithl4"StakeBedfromNational
  Auto Fleet Group, utilizing the Sourcewell Co-Opt Purchasing Program in an amount  not-
  to-exceed $224,359; and
  b.  Authorizing the City Manager to execute the documents necessary to purchase one (l)
  2024 Rizon with 14" stakebed in a form acceptable to the City Attorney.

  FISCAL IMPACT:  There is no impact to the General Fund. The purchase of the 2024 Rizon
  Stake Bed is inthe amount of $224,359. It is budgeted in the Fiscal Year 2025/26 0perating Budget
  with  Fleet  Funds.

  ANALYSIS:  The Public Works Department, Street and Sewer Division, is responsible for
  maintaining the City of South Gate's ("City")  streets and essential infrastructure. This work
  includes asphalt and concrete repairs, street sign maintenance, bulky item cleanups, sewer system
  upkeep, and tree maintenance. Reliable vehicles and equipment are critical for completing these
  tasks efficiently and for providing the high level of service residents expect every day.

  The unit scheduled for replacement (Unit No. 204) is over 32 years old and has exceeded its
  recommended service life. It now requires frequent maintenance, consumes  more  fuel, and
  produces higher emissions than modern vehicles. Its age and declining reliability increase the risk
  of delays in emergency response and routine maintenance operations.

  The replacement vehicle will be :tully electric, which will significantly  reduce fuel costs,
  emissions, and maintenance expenses compared to the current vehicle. This upgrade not only
  enhances operational efficiency but also supports compliance with California Air Resources Board
  ("C ARB") requirements for the purchase of alternative-powered  fleet vehicles. Transitioning  to

  1

  152
 electric  vehicles  aligns  with  the City's  environmental  goals while  providing  a modern,  reliable
unit to support  daily  operations.

Staff recommends  purchasing  the proposed  2024 Rizon  Stake Bed truck  through  the cooperative
contract  purchasing  program  offered  by Sourcewell  (formerly  known  as the National  Joint Powers
Alliance),  rinder  contract  #091521-NAF.  This program  leverages  the national  purchasing  power
of over 50,000  member  agencies,  streamlining  the procurement  process  and reducing  the time and
effort  required  for the City.  Sourcewell  establishes  and provides  competitively  solicited  contracts
in accordance  with  the Uniform  Municipal  Contracting  Law,  ensuring  compliance  with  legal  and
competitive  standards.  This  method  of  purchasing  aligns  with  the  City's  Municipal  Code
requirements  outlined  in Section  1.54.510D,  which  allows  the City to utilize  contracts  established
by other  government  agencies,  avoiding  the need to repeat the competitive  bidding  process.

BACKGROUND:  The Public  Works  Department  operates  a fleet of 90 vehicles  that are essential
for maintaining  and operating  the City's  infrastructure,  including  streets,  sewers,  water  systems,
and emergency  response  functions.  The reliability  of this  fleet  is critical  to ensuring  that crews
can respond  promptly  to resident  service  requests,  maintain  infrastructure  efficiently,  and address
rinplanned  events  such as traffic  hazards,  storm  debris,  or water main  breaks.

To manage  the fleet  effectively,  the Department  developed  a Fleet  Master  Plan ("Plan"),  which
provides  a structured  approach  to reducing  long-term  operating  and maintenance  costs, ensuring
vehicle  safety  and  reliability,  and  increasing  operational  efficiency.  The  Plan  establishes
recommended  vehicle  replacement  cycles  designed  to achieve  the lowest  total  cost of ownership.
Vehicles  kept in service  beyond  their life cycle o:[ten experience  increased  downtime,  higher  repair
costs, greater 'fuel consumption,  and higher  emissions.  Modern  vehicles  provide  not only improved
reliability  and fuel  efficiency  but  also  enhanced  safety  features,  such  as backup  cameras  and
proximity  sensors,  that help protect  both employees  and the public.

The unit proposed  for replacement  was identified  in the Plan for replacement  in 2021, making  this
action  overdue.  The truck  is critical  to the Street and Sewer Division's  daily  operations,  including
delivering  street  barricades  in emergencies,  transporting  materials  to job  sites, and loading  and
unloading  concrete  grinding  equipment.  Timely  replacement  is necessary  to ensure that the vehicle
can be deployed  quickly  and reliably,  particularly  during  emergencies  and for  essential  street
maintenance  operations.

  requirements,  the city is actively  pursuing  a design  to treat it.
